title: Build
content:
The framework reads your attributes in a build step and turns them into a manifest (see Concepts). During development it runs that step itself on each request that needs it. You can also run it from the command line, which is useful in two situations:

To check your code. The build reports every problem it finds: a constructor parameter the container cannot fill, a REST route without permission, an invalid attribute, a typo in a block template. Running it before a commit or in CI catches mistakes without opening WordPress.

To write a release manifest. The release build uses it internally.

vendor/bin/wp-app-framework build [--output=<file>]

In a consumer created as in Getting started, composer build-manifest runs the same command.

Checking

Without --output, the command builds and checks the manifest and writes nothing. It builds the project whose vendor/autoload.php the Composer bin proxy loads, which is the project you run it in. Problems are listed with class and parameter names, and the exit code is 1.

If the build succeeds, the command prints what it found, for example:

Manifest OK (theme my-theme): 40 service candidates, 25 services, 3 hooks, 12 routes, 2 template functions, 1 template filters, 8 blocks, 4 CLI commands, 2 cron events, 1 cron tasks, 1 tables, 2 lifecycle methods. Nothing written (no --output).

The CLI commands are the subcommands of WP-CLI commands. Cron events and cron tasks are the recurring events and one-time tasks of Cron events and tasks, and tables are the row classes of Tables.

The command also lists the templates of the project that override templates of the framework.

Checking templates, parts and patterns

A theme writes blocks into files as well: block templates in templates/, template parts in parts/ and patterns in patterns/. WordPress reads these files as they are. A misspelled attribute, a value the block does not know or HTML in a block that stores none would only show up when the page renders, or not at all, because WordPress drops what it cannot use without a word. The build therefore checks these files against the blocks of your theme.

Take a pattern with a card block whose attribute class has a title and a tone enum with the values light and dark:

<?php
/**
 * Title: Teaser
 * Slug: my-theme/teaser
 */
?>
<!-- wp:my-theme/card {"titel":"Welcome","tone":"pink"} /-->

The build stops with two errors, each with the file, the line and the block:

patterns/teaser.php:6: block my-theme/card: unknown attribute "titel".
patterns/teaser.php:6: block my-theme/card: attribute "tone": "pink" is not one of "light", "dark".

What is checked

The build reads every *.html below templates/ and parts/ and every *.php below patterns/, the files WordPress uses for a block theme. Each block of your theme is checked against its definition. The JSON in the block comment may only contain the attributes of the attribute class and of the block supports, each with a value that fits its schema: the right type, a value of the enum, the required properties of a value class and no others.

The block's structure is checked too. HTML between the block comments is only allowed in a block with a postContent field. Inner blocks are only allowed in a block whose render() takes $content, and only blocks it allows (#[InnerBlocks(allowed)]). A block with parent must sit directly in one of those blocks, a block with ancestor somewhere inside one. A container whose template is locked with TemplateLock::All or TemplateLock::ContentOnly must hold the blocks of its template, because the editor replaces differing inner blocks (see Container blocks).

Template parts and patterns with a single top-level block open in contentOnly mode in the editor (see Content in contentOnly mode). There, a block can only be inserted into a container that is itself a content block. A container of your theme without content that holds content blocks of your theme is therefore an error in such a template part or pattern; give it #[Supports(contentRole: true)].

Blocks of others

The build knows only the blocks of your own theme. Core blocks, blocks of plugins and, in a child theme, the blocks of the parent theme are not checked, because their definitions are not part of your build. Only their JSON must be valid.

A block name in the namespace of your theme (extra.wp-app-framework.namespace) must be one of your blocks: with the namespace my-theme, my-theme/crad is reported as an unknown block. Each theme and plugin has a namespace of its own, so the build can tell your blocks from those of others.

Plugins are not checked, because WordPress reads block templates, template parts and patterns from themes only. A child theme without code has no build, so nothing checks its files.

PHP in patterns

WordPress runs a pattern file as PHP and uses its output. The build cannot run it, so it reads the file as it is and skips the PHP code. PHP in the text of a block, such as a translated sentence in a core paragraph, is fine. PHP inside the block comment of one of your blocks is an error, because the attributes are then only known at run time. Write them as plain JSON.

Rules

The build reports these errors in block templates, template parts and patterns:

A block comment that WordPress would treat as HTML, such as <!--wp:my-theme/card /--> without a space.

A closing comment without an opening one, a closing comment for another block than the open one, and a block that is never closed. WordPress repairs these silently.

Invalid JSON in a block comment, for any block, unless the comment contains PHP. WordPress ignores all attributes of such a block.

An unknown block in the namespace of your own blocks.

In your own blocks:
an attribute that is neither in the attribute class, nor one of the block's supports, nor one of WordPress' attributes allowed by #[Supports] (lock and metadata always; className unless customClassName: false; anchor with anchor: true; align with one of the allowed alignments or ""; style unless customCSS: false);

a value with the wrong type, a value outside the enum, a missing required property or an unknown property of a value class;

the postContent field in the JSON instead of between the block comments;

HTML between the block comments without a postContent field;

inner blocks in a block without $content, and inner blocks missing from #[InnerBlocks(allowed)];

a block outside of the blocks in its parent or ancestor;

inner blocks of a container with a locked template (TemplateLock::All or ContentOnly) whose block names differ from the template;

PHP code in the block comment (patterns);

in a template part or a pattern with a single top-level block, a container that is not a content block but holds content blocks of your theme.


A directory block-templates/ or block-template-parts/. WordPress reads these deprecated directories instead of templates/ and parts/ as soon as one of them exists.

During development, the framework rebuilds the manifest when one of these files changes, so an error shows up on the next request.

Generating fields for queries

vendor/bin/wp-app-framework meta-fields <meta class> [--force]
vendor/bin/wp-app-framework table-fields <row class> [--force]

meta-fields writes the class with #[MetaFields] that queries use to filter and sort by the fields of a meta class: {MetaClass}Fields.php, next to the meta class. table-fields does the same for the columns of a row class: {RowClass}Fields.php with #[TableFields]. Neither replaces an existing file unless you pass --force. Unlike the build, the two write into your source code; the result is yours to change and commit.

Tables

The build checks the row classes of your tables – types, primary key, lengths, indexes, earlier names – and reports every declaration that the database could not create, with class and parameter; the rules list them. It also checks every class with #[TableFields] against its row class. The manifest gets the structure of the tables, a hash of it and the version from the Version: header of your theme or plugin.

Writing a manifest

With --output, the command writes the manifest to the given file. A written manifest is a release manifest and carries the template version, which names the directory of the release's Twig cache.

Do not write generated/manifest.php into a source checkout of a theme or plugin. Its presence switches the project to release mode (see Boot and modes), and the framework stops noticing changes to your code. The release build writes it into its own copy of the project.

title: Releases and CI
content:
Releasing a theme or plugin should be a single step: push a tag. The framework provides a GitHub Actions workflow that does the rest. It builds the release ZIP, installs it into a plain WordPress, runs your browser tests against it, and attaches the ZIP to the GitHub release only if everything passed. A ZIP that fails its tests is never published.

Tags follow semantic versioning with a v prefix: v1.2.0.

Themes, child themes and plugins

Your repository calls the reusable workflow .github/workflows/consumer-release.yml of the framework repository from a workflow of its own. That workflow runs on push: tags: ['v*'] and needs permissions: contents: write to attach the ZIP. The test projects theme-dev-test, theme-dev-test-child and plugin-dev-test contain working examples to copy.

Pin the workflow to a framework tag, so a new framework version never changes your release process unannounced.

The workflow:

checks out the project and wp-test-env, the test environment it runs in;

runs composer lint and npm run lint, if they are defined, and wp-app-framework build;

builds the release; when it publishes, with --expect-version set to the version of the tag, so a tag that doesn't match Version: fails;

installs the ZIP into fresh, plain WordPress instances of wp-test-env, with the plugin and theme directories read-only;

with the input cli-tests: true, runs the project's WP-CLI tests against the installed release (see below);

runs the project's browser tests (npm run test:e2e) with E2E_TARGET=release, one Playwright worker per instance (input e2e-instances, default 2); the input e2e: false skips them.

Plugins and child themes need a theme

A theme can be tested on its own, but a plugin or a child theme needs a theme to run in. The workflow decides from the type in composer.json and the Template: header of style.css:

a plugin is installed next to the release ZIP of a theme;

a child theme is installed on top of the release ZIP of its parent theme.

The input with-theme: <owner>/<repository>@<tag> names that theme release. It is required for plugins and child themes.

WP-CLI tests

Browser tests can't run WP-CLI commands. With cli-tests: true, the workflow runs the executable tests/cli/run of your project after the release is installed. Its only argument is the name of the wp-test-env instance with the release; wp-test-env is checked out next to your project. The script runs your commands with ../wp-test-env/bin/wp "$1" … (relative to your project) and fails with a non-zero exit code if an output or exit code is not what you expect. During development, run the same script against an instance of wp-test-env in development mode.

Browser tests

The workflow runs the browser tests with bin/e2e of wp-test-env: npm run test:e2e of your project in the Playwright image of its @playwright/test version. Every instance gets its own Playwright worker, so tests of different workers never share a site. Your Playwright configuration receives the instance URLs in WP_BASE_URLS (comma-separated), the administrator in WP_USERNAME and WP_PASSWORD, E2E_TARGET and a writable results directory in E2E_OUTPUT_DIR; it sets workers to the number of URLs and lets each worker pick its URL by TEST_PARALLEL_INDEX. The README of wp-test-env explains the contract; the configurations of the test projects are working examples.

Inputs

Input	Default	Purpose
repository	the calling repository	the project to release
ref	the calling ref, i.e. the tag	the revision to build
e2e	true	run the browser tests (npm run test:e2e) against the release
cli-tests	false	run the WP-CLI tests tests/cli/run against the release
publish	true	attach the ZIP to the GitHub release of the tag
framework-ref	the locked version	build with another revision of the framework (the framework's release gate uses it)
e2e-instances	2	number of WordPress instances and Playwright workers for the browser tests
wp-test-env-ref	main	the revision of wp-test-env that provides the tools and the WordPress instances
with-theme	–	the theme release for plugins and child themes, <owner>/<repository>@<tag>

The framework

The framework repository tests itself in two workflows:

ci.yml runs PHPUnit, Vitest and all linters on pushes and pull requests, and builds this documentation.

release.yml runs on a tag. It runs the same checks and then the release gates: theme-dev-test, plugin-dev-test and theme-dev-test-child are built with the framework of the tag (framework-ref) and tested in the browser, the plugin and the child theme with an older release of the theme, without publishing anything. Only then does it attach wp-app-framework-<version>.zip to the GitHub release – made with git archive, without the development files marked export-ignore – and publish the documentation of the tag's minor version.

The gates make sure that a framework release works for a theme, a plugin and a child theme before anyone can depend on it.

Requiring the framework

The framework is on Packagist. Packagist reads the tags of the GitHub repository and updates itself on every push, so a release can be required as soon as its tag exists. Themes and plugins require a version range, and the lock file pins the exact version:

"require": {"saij/wp-app-framework": "^0.15"}

The test projects of the framework require dev-main instead, so they always build with the latest framework.

title: Release
content:
A framework theme or plugin cannot simply be zipped from its Git checkout. The checkout has no vendor/, the editor scripts are not built, and the dependencies are not prefixed. A site with two framework consumers would load one framework for both of them.

wp-app-framework release turns a checkout into a ZIP that runs in any plain WordPress installation, without Composer on the server. It ships all dependencies, including the framework and Twig, prefixed with the project's own namespace in vendor-prefixed/. Several consumers with different framework versions can therefore run side by side.

vendor/bin/wp-app-framework release [--output=<zip>] [--expect-version=<version>] [--package-source=<package>=<directory>]...

In a consumer created as in Getting started, composer release runs the same command. It recognizes a theme or a plugin by the type in its composer.json.

What the release build does

The command works on a copy in the system's temporary directory and never changes your checkout. It runs these steps:

Copy the project. It copies the files Git does not ignore (git ls-files --cached --others --exclude-standard), so uncommitted changes are included. generated/manifest.php must not exist in the checkout.

Install the dependencies. It runs composer install --no-dev --classmap-authoritative from the lock file, so the release contains exactly the versions you tested.

Prefix the dependencies. Strauss renames every dependency into the project's namespace and rewrites the project's own code to use the new names. Strauss must be in the PATH (the tools images of wp-dev-env and wp-test-env provide it); the release command runs it with PHP and a memory limit of 512 MB, since it parses the large class map of the dependencies.
Then the command patches Twig. Twig's compiler writes class names such as use Twig\Environment; as plain strings into every compiled template, and no prefixing tool rewrites strings. Release\TwigPatcher rewrites exactly these places. It expects each pattern a fixed number of times, so a Twig update that changes them fails the build instead of producing a broken release.

Build the manifest. It builds generated/manifest.php with the prefixed classes (using bin/wp-app-framework-prefixed.php in the prefixed copy) and writes the template version into it, and the image variants the templates ask for into generated/assets/ (with Imagick or GD of the PHP that runs the release). Then it compiles all templates of the project and the framework, as release mode would, and checks the compiled code for names that were not prefixed.

Build the assets. If there is a package.json, it runs npm ci && npm run build, which also builds the editor runtime from vendor/. Then it checks that every built file the framework loads at run time exists, because a missing one would only fail on the page that needs it. The manifest decides which files these are:
The project has	It needs in build/
blocks, post meta or editor scripts in assets/	vendor/wp-app-framework/editor.asset.php (editor runtime)
blocks	vendor/wp-app-framework/canvas.asset.php (canvas styles)
an editor or view script of a block or block support	that script's .asset.php
a document view, an editor script or a shared module in assets/	that script's .asset.php below assets/
view scripts or document views	vendor/wp-app-framework/view.asset.php (view runtime)
settings groups	vendor/wp-app-framework/settings.asset.php (settings page)
post meta	vendor/wp-app-framework/meta-box.asset.php (meta boxes)
assets/styles.css	styles.css
fonts marked for preloading in assets/styles.css	styles.preload.php
Static assets in assets/ and the image variants in generated/assets/ are checked as well. A missing file stops the release with a list of the missing files and what needs them. A project without blocks, post meta, settings and stylesheet needs no package.json; one with them needs a package.json with a build script and a webpack.config.js with the framework's webpack helper.

Remove development files. It removes node_modules/, vendor/, composer.json, composer.lock, package.json, package-lock.json and every path the project marks export-ignore in .gitattributes (use dir/** for directories). Then it checks all PHP files for names of dependencies that were not prefixed, in string literals too. Inside vendor-prefixed/ string literals are not checked, because dependencies mention their own class names in messages.

Write the ZIP. It writes dist/<slug>-<version>.zip, or the file given with --output, with the project directory as root. The slug is the directory name. The version is the Version: header of the theme's or child theme's style.css, or of the plugin's main file <slug>.php. --expect-version makes the build fail if the version differs, which CI uses to compare it with the tag.

A child theme is built without its parent theme. Calls of the parent's public template callables compile without it.

Every step fails with the file, command or setting at fault. On failure the build directory is kept, and its path is printed, so you can look at what went wrong.

Strauss settings

The project declares the Strauss settings in its composer.json. The command cannot add them itself, because extra is part of the lock file's content hash. It checks the values it relies on instead:

"extra": {
    "strauss": {
        "target_directory": "vendor-prefixed",
        "namespace_prefix": "Vendor\\Theme\\Vendor\\",
        "classmap_prefix": "Vendor_Theme_Vendor_",
        "include_root_autoload": true,
        "update_call_sites": ["src", "functions.php"],
        "delete_vendor_packages": false
    }
}

namespace_prefix and classmap_prefix name the prefix for the dependencies. The prefix must not be the project's own namespace, which is Strauss' default.

update_call_sites lists where Strauss rewrites your code to the prefixed names. It must contain the file that boots the framework: functions.php of a theme or child theme, <slug>.php of a plugin.

Leave constant_prefix unset. It would rename the constants that the Symfony polyfills define for PHP itself, such as MB_CASE_UPPER. Twig defines no constants.

Unreleased framework changes

Normally the release uses the framework version from the lock file. To test a release with framework changes that are not released yet, replace the package with a local checkout:

composer release -- --package-source=saij/wp-app-framework=../wp-app-framework

--package-source=<package>=<directory> copies the checkout's files without those marked export-ignore, like a distribution archive. The output says that the build is not from the lock file. Composer path repositories are not supported, because the temporary copy has no sibling checkouts.

Distribution

The release ZIP is what you hand on – the source checkout never goes to a site. Where it goes depends on what you built.

A plugin that others may use belongs in the plugin directory of WordPress.org. You commit the content of the release ZIP to the plugin's SVN repository. The directory requires every file of a plugin to be under a license compatible with the GPL; the framework, Twig and the release build meet that, as long as your own code does too. Sites built with Bedrock then install the plugin with Composer from a mirror of the directory, such as repo.wp-packages.org, like any other plugin from WordPress.org.

A theme built with the framework cannot go into the theme directory of WordPress.org. Its review requirements forbid custom blocks and custom post types in themes, and blocks are what a framework theme is made of. A theme built for one site therefore lives in that site's repository – in a Bedrock site under web/app/themes/<slug> – and the deployment builds its release there:

cd web/app/themes/my-theme && composer release

The release command works in a subdirectory of another repository: it collects the files of the theme's directory with Git. The deployment then puts the content of the ZIP in place of the theme's source directory. The same applies to a plugin that only one site uses.

Rules:

The release ZIP contains the directory <slug>/ with everything the theme or plugin needs; nothing is installed on the server.

The framework and its dependencies are licensed under the GPL-2.0-or-later; a theme or plugin that ships them must be GPL-compatible as well.

Never deploy the source checkout: it runs in development mode, with unprefixed classes and without the release build's checks.

title: Concepts
content:
This page explains the ideas that the rest of the documentation relies on: who uses the framework, what happens in the build and what happens at run time, and how a block travels from a PHP class to the page and to the editor. You don't need it to follow Getting started, but the guides make more sense once you know it.

Consumers and instances

The framework is a Composer library. A project that includes it is a consumer. There are three kinds:

a theme, which boots the framework with Theme::boot();

a plugin, which boots it with Plugin::boot(__FILE__);

a child theme with code of its own (blocks, hooks, REST routes), which boots it with ChildTheme::boot(). A child theme that only overrides templates and adjusts theme.json needs no framework code at all.

Every consumer that boots creates its own instance of the framework. Instances are strictly separated, so everything with a global name is derived from one of two names of the consumer.

The namespace names what your content and data refer to. You choose it once in composer.json, as extra.wp-app-framework.namespace, for example sections. Your blocks are registered as sections/hero, your REST routes live under sections/v1, your WP-CLI commands under wp sections, your settings are stored in options such as sections_general, and your post types, taxonomies and meta keys are named sections_event and the like. These names end up in posts and in the database, so they must stay the same for as long as the content exists.

The slug is the directory name of the theme or plugin. It names the technical parts: the REST route of the editor, the script handles, the JavaScript global window.wpAppFramework[slug], the cache directory wp-content/cache/{slug}/ and the init action wp_app_framework/init/{slug}. The directory name can change when a theme or plugin is installed under another name; that's why no content depends on it.

Two consumers that boot with the same slug or the same namespace are an error.

The separation goes further in a release. Each consumer ships its own copy of the framework and its dependencies, prefixed with its own namespace. A theme built with framework 0.6 and a plugin built with 0.7 load different classes and don't interfere with each other. The flip side is that instances cannot pass framework objects to each other. When a plugin wants to offer something to the theme, it does so through a public interface made of WordPress filters named after its slug (see Plugins).

Build and run time

You declare almost everything with PHP attributes: #[Hook] on a method registers a hook, #[RestRoute] a REST route, #[Block] a block, #[TemplateFunction] a Twig function, #[SettingsGroup] a group of settings, #[PostType] a post type, #[Table] a database table. Nothing reads these attributes while WordPress handles a request in production. Instead, a build step reads them once and writes a manifest: plain PHP data listing the hooks, routes, blocks with their attribute schemas, template functions, settings and the services with their constructor dependencies.

This has two benefits. First, mistakes surface early. A REST route without a permission, a constructor parameter the container cannot fill, a template function with the name of a Twig built-in – each is a build error naming the class at fault, not a surprise in production. Second, a release does no extra work at run time: it loads the manifest and calls your classes, without reflection, without checking files, and without ever writing into the theme or plugin directory.

You can run the checks yourself at any time with composer build-manifest (see Build).

Development mode and release mode

You don't run the build by hand while you develop. The framework picks one of two modes:

Release mode applies when the consumer contains generated/manifest.php. Only the release build writes that file, so this is what runs on a live site.

Development mode applies otherwise, for example in your Git checkout. The framework builds the manifest itself on the first request and caches it in wp-content/cache/{slug}/manifest/. On each request it checks whether your classes changed in a way that matters – a new attribute, a changed signature – and rebuilds only then. You edit a file and reload the page.

Boot and modes describes both modes in detail.

Services

Your classes don't create each other. Concrete classes in your PSR-4 directories are service candidates (with a few exceptions such as enums and attribute classes), and the framework's container creates them when needed, passing other services into their constructors. A class that has a hook, a REST route, a template function or filter, or a block is an entry point; everything it needs is created for it, and only when the hook fires, the route is called or the block renders. See Services.

How a block works

Blocks show how these pieces fit together. A block consists of three files next to each other:

src/Block/Teaser/
├── Teaser.php             the block: #[Block] and a render() method
├── TeaserAttributes.php   the attributes as a typed class
└── Teaser.twig            the markup

Two optional scripts can sit next to them: Teaser.editor.js extends the block in the editor (see Editor), Teaser.view.js gives it behavior on the page (see Front-end scripts).

In the build, the framework reads the attribute class and derives the attribute schema from its constructor: types, defaults, the allowed values of enums, and which attributes are content. There is no block.json. On init the framework registers the block with register_block_type(), and WordPress passes the definition to the block editor by itself.

In the post content, the block is stored as a comment with its attributes as JSON:

<!-- wp:my-theme/teaser {"title":"Summer party","highlighted":true} /-->

On the front end, WordPress calls the framework when it renders the block. The framework cleans the attributes against their schema, turns them into an instance of your attribute class, and calls your block's render() method, which renders the Twig template.

In the editor, the framework's editor runtime asks the server to render the block from the same template. The template marks editable elements with field('title'). In the editor these marks become attributes on the element, and the runtime replaces the marked elements with text editors, image pickers and inner blocks. Content editors type into the real markup; there is no second template for the editor. Typing does not re-render the block, but every other change, such as a different option in the inspector, does.

With #[Cache], the front end renders the block once and reads its HTML from the cache until a tag of the block is invalidated or the entry expires. The editor always renders it fresh.

With a front-end script, the block also gets behavior on the page. The framework loads the script only on pages that render the block and starts one instance of its class per block. In the editor, a Preview button in the block's toolbar shows the front-end markup and runs the script on it.

TeaserAttributes.php ──build──▶ attribute schema ──▶ register_block_type()
                                                         │
             post content: <!-- wp:my-theme/teaser {…} /-->
                                                         │
          ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┴───────────────┐
     front end: render() → Teaser.twig → HTML         editor: render route → same HTML
                                                        → marked fields become editors

Blocks and Editor go into the details.

src and assets

Each project has two directories for its own files. src/ holds everything that belongs to a PHP class: the classes themselves, their Twig templates and the scripts of blocks and block supports, each next to its class (Hero.php, Hero.twig, Hero.editor.js, Hero.view.js).

assets/ holds everything that belongs to no PHP class: the stylesheet assets/styles.css (see Styles), scripts for the whole page (*.view.js, see Scripts for the whole page), editor scripts without a block (*.editor.js, see Editor) modules shared between scripts (assets/shared/, see Shared modules) and static files such as images and fonts (see Static assets). The directory is optional and ships with the release like src/.

A script in src/ that sits next to no block or block support class is a build error. The webpack helper would build it, but the framework would never load it.

Templates in layers

Twig templates live in the src/ directory of each project, next to the code that uses them. A template name is always the full path relative to src/, such as Block/Teaser/Teaser.twig.

When the framework looks for a template, it searches several layers in order. For a theme this is the active child theme's overrides/{theme-slug}/, then the theme's src/, then the framework's src/. A file with the same path on a higher layer wins. That is how a child theme changes the markup of a theme's block without touching its code, and how a theme changes the markup of a plugin's block. See Twig templates.

Errors

The framework never hides a missing prerequisite. Missing prerequisites – a missing build output, an unknown template, a wrong boot method – raise exceptions that name the file, class or parameter at fault.

Errors in your code at run time depend on WP_DEBUG. With WP_DEBUG enabled, exceptions from hooks and blocks are rethrown, so you see them immediately. Without it, they are written to the PHP error log, and the site keeps working: a filter returns its original value, a block renders nothing. REST routes always answer with an error response instead (see REST routes), and WP-CLI commands end with an error message (see WP-CLI commands).
description: This page explains the ideas that the rest of the documentation relies on: who uses the framework, what happens in the build and what happens at run time, and how a block travels from a PHP class to the page and to the editor. You don't need it to follow Getting started, but the guides make more sense once you know it.

title: Getting started
description: In this walkthrough you set up a block theme called my-theme and give it a first block: a teaser with a title and a text that content editors type directly into the editor canvas, and a switch in the inspector that highlights it. Along the way you see every file a consumer of the framework needs and why it is there. Plugins and child themes with code of their own are set up the same way. Boot and modes, Plugins and Child themes describe what differs.

description: A theme ships more than code: a logo, icons, placeholder images, a font, a PDF to download. These files live in the assets/ directory of the theme or plugin, next to src/. The framework gives each a URL that changes with its content, prints images with their size and in smaller versions and modern formats, inlines SVG icons, preloads fonts, imports files into the media library and lets a child theme replace a file without code.

title: Blocks
content:
Blocks are the heart of a framework theme. Every block is rendered on the server from a Twig template, and content editors edit it inline in the editor canvas. This page shows how to write a block, which attributes it can have and how its values reach the markup. How blocks are stored A WordPress block usually stores its HTML in the post content. Once saved, that HTML stays as it is: changing the block's markup later means either migrating old posts or leaving them with the old markup. Framework blocks store no markup. The post content holds only the block comment with the attributes as JSON: When the page is displayed, the framework renders the block from its Twig template. A change to the template therefore shows up in every post at once. Block supports such as alignment or an anchor are attributes as well. There is one exception: the value of a #[RichText(postContent: true)] field is stored as inline HTML without a wrapping element, e.g. Summer party. That keeps the text of paragraphs and headings in the post content, where search and other plugins expect it (see Text in the post content). Anatomy of a block A block is made of three parts: a service class with #[Block] and a render() method, a typed attribute class, and a Twig template. There is no block.json. The build derives the attribute schema from the attribute class, and WordPress passes it to the editor on its own (through get_block_editor_server_block_settings()). The schema and the PHP object you work with therefore always match. Here is a hero block with a topline, a headline, an image, a gradient and a list of buttons. The block class use Saij\WpAppFramework\Block\Align; use Saij\WpAppFramework\Block\Block; use Saij\WpAppFramework\Block\BlockCategory; use Saij\WpAppFramework\Block\Supports; use Saij\WpAppFramework\Twig\TemplateRenderer; #[Block('hero', title: 'Hero', category: BlockCategory::Design, icon: 'cover-image')] #[Supports(anchor: true, align: [Align::Wide, Align::Full])] final class Hero { public function __construct(private readonly TemplateRenderer $renderer) { } public function render(HeroAttributes $attrs, string $content, WP_Block $block): string { return $this->renderer->render('Block/Hero/Hero.twig', ['attrs' => $attrs, 'content' => $content]); } } #[Block] names the block and describes it for the inserter. #[Supports] switches on WordPress features: here an HTML anchor and the wide and full alignments. render() receives what it asks for. HeroAttributes is the attribute object, string $content the rendered inner blocks, and WP_Block $block WordPress' block instance. A block that asks for $content can contain inner blocks (see Container blocks). The attribute class use Saij\WpAppFramework\Block\Content; use Saij\WpAppFramework\Block\Image; use Saij\WpAppFramework\Block\Label; use Saij\WpAppFramework\Block\PlainText; use Saij\WpAppFramework\Block\RichText; use Saij\WpAppFramework\Value\ListOf; use Saij\WpAppFramework\Value\Url; final readonly class HeroAttributes { public function __construct( #[PlainText] public string $topline = '', #[RichText(allowedFormats: ['core/bold', 'core/italic'])] public string $headline = '', #[Image] #[Label('Image')] public ?int $imageId = null, public Gradient $gradient = Gradient::Black, #[ListOf(Button::class)] public array $buttons = [], ) { } } final readonly class Button { public function __construct( #[PlainText] public string $label, #[Content] #[Url] public string $url = '', ) { } } Each constructor parameter becomes an attribute, and its type decides how it is edited: $topline and $headline are edited in the canvas: plain text, and rich text with bold and italic. $imageId is an image chosen from the media library in the canvas. Only the attachment ID is stored. $gradient is a backed enum. The editor shows a select with its cases in the inspector. $buttons is a list of Button value objects. The inspector shows a list editor, and each button's label is edited in the canvas. The template
{% if attrs.topline or is_editor() %} {{ attrs.topline }}

{% endif %} {{ attrs.headline|raw }} {{ wp_attachment_image(attrs.imageId, 'large') }} {% for button in attrs.buttons %} {{ button.label }} {% endfor %} {{ content|raw }}
The template is ordinary Twig with a few helpers: block_wrapper_attributes() goes on the root element. It adds the classes and the anchor of the block's supports, and the marker of its front-end scripts. field('topline') marks the element that shows a field, so the editor can turn it into an editor. inner_blocks() marks where inner blocks go. is_editor() keeps the empty topline in the editor, so content editors can fill it in, while the front end leaves it out. On the front end field(), inner_blocks() and is_editor() print nothing; they only matter in the editor (see Editor). The headline is printed with |raw because it holds HTML; everything else is escaped by Twig (see Escaping). #[Block] #[Block(name, title, category, icon: '', description: '', keywords: [], usesContext: [], excerptWrapper: false, parent: null, ancestor: null)] goes on a service class. The name is the name of the block without namespace, in lowercase letters, digits and -, for example hero. The framework registers it in the namespace of your theme or plugin (extra.wp-app-framework.namespace in composer.json, see Concepts): with the namespace sections, hero becomes sections/hero. That full name is what WordPress stores in posts and what you write in templates, patterns and filters. A name with / and duplicate names are build errors. The framework itself declares no blocks. The category is a BlockCategory case for the categories of WordPress, or a case of an enum of your own (see Categories); an enum instead of a string lets your IDE complete it. usesContext lists the context values of other blocks the block reads from WP_Block::$context. The typical case is postId in a query loop, where a block shows data of the current post. Values of your own containers are read with #[Context] instead. parent and ancestor limit where the block can be inserted: directly into one of the named blocks, or anywhere inside them (see Container blocks). Which blocks a container accepts, its template and its lock are declared with #[InnerBlocks]. excerptWrapper adds a container to WordPress' excerpt_allowed_wrapper_blocks (see Excerpts). It also requires string $content. The framework registers blocks on init with api_version 3. #[Supports] #[Supports] switches on the block supports of WordPress. Its arguments and their defaults are WordPress' own: #[Supports(contentRole: false, anchor: false, align: [], customClassName: true, multiple: true, reusable: true, inserter: true, lock: true, renaming: true, customCSS: true)] Only values that differ from WordPress' defaults are registered. html is always disabled, because a framework block has no stored HTML to edit. contentRole: true is for container blocks without content of their own. WordPress 7 opens patterns and template parts in contentOnly mode, where editors may only insert blocks into containers that count as content. A block counts as content if it has a content attribute (see Fields) or contentRole: true. A section that only holds inner blocks needs contentRole: true, so that blocks can be inserted into it in contentOnly mode. The build reports a container without it in your patterns and template parts. customCSS, enabled by default in WordPress 7, lets users with edit_css store free CSS for each block instance. Whether to allow that is the theme's decision: per block with customCSS: false, or for all blocks with a register_block_type_args hook of its own. Settings of your own that several blocks share, such as a color scheme, are block supports of the theme or plugin, added with #[UseSupport]. render() render() is public, non-static and returns string. Its parameters are matched by type, each at most once and in any order: the attribute class, string – the rendered inner blocks, WP_Block – WordPress' block instance, parameters marked with #[Context] – values an enclosing block passes on. Services come through the constructor. The block service is created when the block renders for the first time, not when WordPress registers it. Attribute class The attribute class is a value class (see Values). Every parameter needs a default value, because any attribute can be missing in the content: the block was inserted before the attribute existed, or the editor never set it. Some names are taken. WordPress adds the attributes lock, metadata, className, anchor, align and style itself (style comes with the customCSS support, enabled by default in WordPress 7). The attributes of the block's own block supports are taken as well. None of these can be a parameter of the attribute class. From the class, the build creates the attribute schema with type, enum, properties/items, default and role: content (see below). Fields Most blocks hold text and images that content editors should change directly where they see them. Mark these parameters, and the editor makes them editable in the canvas: #[PlainText] – inline text, on strings only. #[RichText(allowedFormats: null)] – inline HTML, on strings only. allowedFormats lists the formats the editor offers, e.g. ['core/bold']; null allows all, [] none. #[Image] – an attachment ID, on ?int only. Some values are not visible in the markup, or are better edited in a form. With inspector: true – #[RichText(inspector: true)], also on #[PlainText] and #[Image] – a field is edited in the block inspector instead of the canvas. An address or a short poem needs line breaks. #[PlainText(multiline: true)] allows them: in the canvas, Enter and Shift+Enter insert a line break, and with inspector: true the inspector shows a text area. The value contains \n; print it with |nl2br, which escapes the text before it adds
:

{{ attrs.address|nl2br }}

The canvas shows a line break at the very end of the text as an empty line, the front end does not. A Link is a link to a post, term or media file, or a free URL. It has its own control in the inspector and counts as content. #[Content] marks other content, such as the URL of a link. It is edited in the inspector like any other value, but it counts as content: its control appears in the inspector's "Content" group, and WordPress keeps it editable in contentOnly mode (see below). References to posts, terms and users (#[PostReference], #[TermReference], #[UserReference]) are edited with a search in the inspector, and they count as content too. Content in contentOnly mode In WordPress 7, template parts and inserted patterns open in contentOnly mode. Content editors can change the content of blocks there, but not their design. A pattern becomes such a section only if it has a single top-level block, such as a group around its content; WordPress inserts a pattern with several top-level blocks as ordinary blocks. A block without content attributes is still shown, but it cannot be selected. WordPress decides by the attribute's role: content. The build sets it for you: an attribute gets role: content if it, or a field nested in it, carries #[PlainText], #[RichText], #[Image] or #[Content], or is a reference or a Link. In the example, buttons is content because each button has a label and a URL. The marks have no effect on REST arguments. Editor labels The editor needs a label for each value. #[Label('…')] sets the label in the inspector and the placeholder of an inline field. Without it, the label is derived from the parameter name: imageId becomes "Image id". A backed enum labels its cases by implementing Block\Labeled with a method label(): string. The build evaluates it, so it may not depend on run-time state. Without it, the editor shows the case values. #[Hidden] keeps a value out of the generated inspector. It is not allowed on inline fields. Text in the post content Text blocks such as paragraphs and headings are a special case. Search, SEO plugins and exports read the raw post content, and for most blocks they find only JSON there. For a block whose whole purpose is text, it is better to keep the text in the post content. #[RichText(postContent: true)] does that. The value is stored as the block's inner HTML instead of in the block comment: inline HTML without a wrapping element. The markup around it still comes from Twig. final readonly class ParagraphAttributes { public function __construct( #[RichText(postContent: true)] public string $text = '', ) {} }

{{ attrs.text|raw }}

As the example shows, the root element of the template may be the field itself. For your code nothing changes: the template prints the value like any other. Under the hood, the attribute is a sourced attribute (source: html without selector), and the editor saves it with RawHTML. WordPress never parses sourced attributes on the server, so the framework takes the value from the block content before it creates the attribute object. The following are build errors, each for a reason: The field is not a parameter of the attribute class itself (but of a value class or a list item): only top-level values can map to the inner HTML. A block has more than one such field: there is only one inner HTML. The block has inner blocks: inner blocks and the field would share the block content. The default is not '': the editor stores an empty value as empty block content. Excerpts WordPress creates automatic excerpts from the post content – for archives, core/post-excerpt, feeds and REST – when a post has no manual excerpt (get_the_excerpt()). To do that, it renders only blocks that it knows contain text. Framework blocks tell WordPress which of their texts belong in an excerpt. excerpt: true on #[PlainText] or #[RichText] includes the value in automatic excerpts. It also works in list items, in value classes and with inspector: true. Blocks with such fields are added to excerpt_allowed_blocks. When WordPress renders a block for an excerpt, the block renders only its excerpt fields, one paragraph each: rich text as stored, plain text escaped. Neither render() nor the template runs. wp_trim_excerpt() then strips the tags. WordPress renders blocks for an excerpt while the get_the_excerpt filter runs, and offers no other signal. If other code renders blocks inside a get_the_excerpt filter, framework blocks render as excerpts there, too. WordPress never renders blocks with inner blocks for excerpts, so excerpt: true in such a block is a build error. For a container, use #[Block(excerptWrapper: true)] instead. It includes the excerpts of the container's allowed inner blocks, like core/group. Search Search is unchanged. WordPress searches the raw post content, and it finds single words of values in the block comment JSON, which stores non-ASCII characters as they are. It does not find phrases across formatting, nor values with &, <, > or " (stored as & etc.). Attribute names and enum values match, too. Categories The inserter groups blocks by category. WordPress brings six (BlockCategory: text, media, design, widgets, theme, embed). A theme with many blocks of its own usually wants its own categories, so editors find them at once. Declare them as a string backed enum that implements CustomBlockCategory. Each case is a category; label() is its title in the inserter and icon() the name of a dashicon shown next to it, or null: enum Category: string implements CustomBlockCategory { case Sections = 'sections'; case Teasers = 'teasers'; public function label(): string { return match ($this) { self::Sections => 'Sections', self::Teasers => 'Teasers', }; } public function icon(): ?string { return $this === self::Sections ? 'layout' : null; } } #[Block('hero', title: 'Hero', category: Category::Sections)] The framework registers every case of each enum a block uses, before the categories of WordPress: enums in the order of their class names, the cases in their order. The slug of a category is {namespace}-{value}, here sections-sections for the namespace sections. The build reports a value other than lowercase letters, digits and -, an empty label and an empty icon (return null instead). Inserter preview When an editor hovers a block in the inserter, WordPress shows a preview of it. The preview renders the block like the canvas does. Without further declarations the preview shows the block with its default attributes, and a container with the template of its #[InnerBlocks]. #[Example] sets the values instead: #[Block('hero', title: 'Hero', category: Category::Sections)] #[Example(attributes: ['headline' => 'Spring sale', 'tone' => Tone::Dark], viewportWidth: 1200)] #[Example(attributes: [], innerBlocks: [], viewportWidth: null)] takes the attribute values (a backed enum stands for its value), the inner blocks as TemplateBlock and the width in pixels the preview is rendered at (WordPress uses 500). #[Example(false)] shows no preview. The build checks the attribute values against the attribute class and reports inner blocks for a block without inner blocks. Variations Some blocks come in a few typical setups: a dark hero, tabs with three tabs. A variation offers such a setup in the editor under a title of its own, without a block of its own. The post stores the block with the preset attributes, so the variation is just a starting point. #[Block('hero', title: 'Hero', category: Category::Sections)] #[Variation('dark', 'Dark hero', attributes: ['tone' => Tone::Dark], isActive: ['tone'])] #[Variation] is repeatable. Its arguments are WordPress' own: Argument Meaning name unique within the block; lowercase letters, digits and - title, description, icon, keywords how the inserter shows the variation attributes preset attribute values; a backed enum stands for its value innerBlocks preset inner blocks as TemplateBlock, for containers scope where the editor offers it: VariationScope::Inserter (an item of its own), VariationScope::Block (the placeholder, like the layouts of core/columns), VariationScope::Transform (a switch in the toolbar); default inserter and block isDefault replaces the block itself in the inserter isActive the attributes by which the editor recognizes the variation of a block, to show its title and icon in the block card and the list view; each must be preset in attributes The build checks the attribute values against the attribute class and the inner blocks against the container, and reports invalid or duplicate names and an empty title. Attributes at render time WordPress validates the attributes against the schema before rendering: an invalid value falls back to the default. It checks each attribute as a whole, so a list with one invalid item or a value object with one invalid field falls back to its default completely. It does not sanitize them, though. The framework's value factory therefore sanitizes each attribute against its schema (rest_sanitize_value_from_schema()) and only then creates the attribute object. Attributes of block supports, WordPress' and your own, are not part of the attribute object. Caching A block that queries data can keep its output with #[Cache]: it renders once per attribute set and is read from the cache until a tag is invalidated or its lifetime ends. See Cache. Errors An exception in render() or while the attribute object is created is rethrown if WP_DEBUG is enabled. Otherwise it is logged with error_log(), and the block renders nothing. The rest of the page still renders. Core blocks The framework disables no core blocks. Which ones a theme offers is the theme's decision. A hook on allowed_block_types_all limits them: final class AllowedBlocks { /** * @param bool|list $allowed * @return bool|list */ #[Hook('allowed_block_types_all')] public function filter(bool|array $allowed): bool|array { return ['core/post-content', 'core/template-part', 'sections/hero' /* … */]; } } Escaping Twig escapes every value unless you say otherwise. This table shows how each kind of value gets into the markup: Value Output #[PlainText] and other strings {{ attrs.topline }} – Twig's autoescaping #[PlainText(multiline: true)] {{ attrs.address|nl2br }} – escaped, then line breaks as
#[RichText] {{ attrs.headline|raw }} – exactly as stored; WordPress filters it with wp_kses when a user without unfiltered_html saves #[Url] strings {{ button.url }} – the schema has format: uri, so the value is sanitized with sanitize_url() (disallowed protocols such as javascript: become empty) and then autoescaped Images #[Image] attachment ID with {{ wp_attachment_image(attrs.imageId, size = 'full', attributes = {}) }} (wp_get_attachment_image(); empty for null; more in WordPress functions) Links – href with esc_url(), plus target and rel for a new tab; empty without URL (see Links) References IDs; {{ wp_post_title(attrs.target) }}, {{ wp_post_url(attrs.target) }}, wp_term_name(), wp_term_url(), wp_user_name() and more WordPress functions (see References) Inner blocks {{ content|raw }} Root element {{ block_wrapper_attributes(extra = {}) }} (get_block_wrapper_attributes(): classes and anchor of the supports, plus the classes of block supports and the marker of front-end scripts) Don't apply string filters such as upper to HTML: they change tags, URLs and entities too. Use CSS for uppercase text.

title: Boot and modes
content:
Before the framework can register anything, your theme or plugin has to start it. That takes one call in the file WordPress loads first: functions.php for a theme, the main plugin file for a plugin. This page shows that call for each kind of project. It then explains the two modes the framework runs in: development mode for your checkout and release mode for production.

Boot

Themes

A theme loads Composer's autoloader and boots the framework in its functions.php:

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

// Release builds ship prefixed dependencies in vendor-prefixed/; source checkouts use Composer's vendor/.
require is_file(__DIR__ . '/vendor-prefixed/autoload.php')
    ? __DIR__ . '/vendor-prefixed/autoload.php'
    : __DIR__ . '/vendor/autoload.php';

Saij\WpAppFramework\Theme::boot();

The autoloader lines choose between two directories. In your Git checkout, Composer installs everything into vendor/. A release ZIP contains vendor-prefixed/ instead, with every dependency renamed into the theme's own namespace (see Release). If neither exists, require fails with a fatal error that names the missing path.

Plugins

A plugin does the same in its main file. The main file must be named after the plugin's directory, for example my-plugin/my-plugin.php, and it passes its own path to the boot:

<?php
/**
 * Plugin Name: My Plugin
 * Version: 1.0.0
 * Requires PHP: 8.5
 */

declare(strict_types=1);

require is_file(__DIR__ . '/vendor-prefixed/autoload.php')
    ? __DIR__ . '/vendor-prefixed/autoload.php'
    : __DIR__ . '/vendor/autoload.php';

Saij\WpAppFramework\Plugin::boot(__FILE__);

The framework needs the file to find the plugin's directory and its URL; asset URLs of a plugin come from plugin_dir_url().

Child themes

A child theme without code needs neither a boot nor a build. It overrides templates of its parent theme and adjusts theme.json like any child theme.

A child theme with code of its own – blocks, hooks, REST routes – boots its own framework instance in its functions.php. It uses the same autoloader lines and Saij\WpAppFramework\ChildTheme::boot();. Child themes explains how it works next to its parent theme.

Slug, namespace and init action

Each instance is identified by a slug. For a theme it is get_template(), for a child theme get_stylesheet() and for a plugin its directory name. The framework derives the technical global names of the instance from it: script handles, the JavaScript global, the cache directory and the init action. Blocks, REST routes, WP-CLI commands and settings options use the namespace from composer.json instead (see Concepts).

A slug can boot only once. A second boot with the same slug is an error, whether it comes from the same project or from a theme and a plugin that happen to share a directory name. The same holds for the namespace: when an instance boots, the framework fires the action wp_app_framework/namespace/{namespace}, and a second instance with the same namespace stops with an error.

At the end of the boot the framework fires the action wp_app_framework/init/{slug}, without arguments.

The kind of project

The framework's build reads the kind of project from the type in its composer.json, which must be wordpress-theme or wordpress-plugin. A theme needs a style.css. If that file names a parent theme in its Template: header, the project is a child theme.

Modes

The framework reads your attributes in a build step and writes the result into a manifest (see Concepts). Where that manifest comes from depends on the mode, and the framework chooses the mode by itself. You never set a constant or a flag.

Release mode

A theme or plugin is in release mode when it contains generated/manifest.php. Only the release build creates that file, so release mode is what runs on a live site.

In release mode the framework loads the manifest as it is: no reflection, no file checks, and no writes into the theme or plugin directory. Compiled Twig templates go to a cache directory named after the template version of the release (see Twig templates).

Development mode

Without generated/manifest.php the framework is in development mode. This is the mode of your checkout. You change a class, reload the page, and the change is there.

The framework builds the manifest by reflection and caches it in wp-content/cache/{slug}/manifest/, never in the project itself. To avoid rebuilding on every request, it works like Symfony's container cache in debug mode. A meta file records the files the build depended on, with relative paths only. On each request the framework compares modification times. Only for files that are newer does it recompute the class signature or the file content. The signature covers attributes, parents, interfaces, traits and the signatures of the constructor and public methods; it does not cover method bodies. Only a difference triggers a rebuild, so editing the body of a method costs nothing.

Several consumers in development mode

In development mode the framework and its dependencies are not prefixed. All consumers therefore share the same classes, and whichever autoloader runs first provides them. A plugin built against one framework checkout would silently run with the framework of the theme.

To rule that out, the boot checks two things and fails if either does not hold:

the loaded framework is the consumer's own vendor/saij/wp-app-framework, compared by real path;

the loaded Twig version is the one recorded in the consumer's vendor/composer/installed.php.

In practice, link the same framework checkout into every consumer. The option WP_PACKAGE_LINKS of wp-dev-env does exactly that.

title: Cache
content:
Some work is too expensive to repeat on every request: a block that queries the latest posts, a REST route that adds up statistics, a service that calls an external API. The framework can keep the result and use it again until something changes. You decide what is cached and what a result depends on; the framework stores it, finds it again and throws it away when it is outdated.

This page explains how the cache works, how you cache a block, a REST route and data of your own, and how entries are invalidated.

How it works

Every theme or plugin has a cache of its own, named after its slug. An entry is stored under a key. The framework builds the key from four things:

The inputs. For a block, its attributes, its inner content and the values of the context it uses (usesContext, such as postId). For a REST route, the arguments of the request. For your own data, the key you choose.

The variants. The circumstances you declare the result depends on, such as the logged-in user or a parameter of the URL. Each variant adds its current value to the key, so every value gets an entry of its own.

The tags. Each tag has a version; invalidating a tag gives it a new version, so the entries with that tag are never read again.

The code. New code never reads entries of old code. In release mode the framework uses the version of your PHP code and templates from the release build. In development mode it looks at the modification times of your files, so a changed template or class takes effect on the next request.

An entry also has a lifetime, the ttl in seconds. It expires after that time, even if no tag is invalidated.

Nothing depends on the request unless you say so. If a block shows something different for logged-in users and you declare no variant for it, the first visitor decides what everybody sees until the entry expires. Declare every circumstance the result depends on.

A block, step by step

A block that shows the latest posts queries the database each time it renders. With #[Cache] it renders once and is then read from the cache:

// src/Block/LatestPosts/LatestPosts.php
use Saij\WpAppFramework\Cache\Cache;
use Saij\WpAppFramework\Cache\Tag\PostTypeTag;

#[Block('latest-posts', title: 'Latest posts', category: BlockCategory::Widgets)]
#[Cache(ttl: 3600, tags: [new PostTypeTag('post')])]
final class LatestPosts
{
    public function __construct(private readonly TemplateRenderer $templates) {}

    public function render(LatestPostsAttributes $attrs): string
    {
        $posts = get_posts(['numberposts' => $attrs->count]);

        return $this->templates->render('Block/LatestPosts/LatestPosts.twig', ['attrs' => $attrs, 'posts' => $posts]);
    }
}

The block now renders once per combination of attributes and stays cached for an hour. The PostTypeTag invalidates it as soon as a post is published, changed, trashed or deleted, so a new post shows up right away.

If the block shows a page of the list depending on a URL parameter, declare that parameter as a variant:

#[Cache(ttl: 3600, tags: [new PostTypeTag('post')], vary: [new QueryParamVary('page')])]

Now ?page=2 gets an entry of its own.

The cache is used only on the front end. Renders for the block editor and its preview always run render(), so editors see their changes at once. Excerpts are never cached either.

What a cached block keeps

A block read from the cache skips its template and render(). Everything that ends up in the HTML is kept. Beyond that, the framework keeps one more thing: the scripts, styles and script modules render() enqueues are recorded with the entry and enqueued again when the block comes from the cache. The block's view scripts are enqueued as usual. Register the scripts and styles you enqueue before blocks render, for example on init: when the block comes from the cache, a handle that is not registered is an error.

Other side effects of render() do not happen when the block comes from the cache. Decisions WordPress makes per request are kept as they were, too: WordPress decides loading="lazy" and fetchpriority of images by their order on the page, so a cached block keeps the attributes of the render that stored it. A block with inner blocks caches only its own output; the inner blocks render before it, as always, and their output is part of its input.

Template functions that depend on the request

Some WordPress functions in Twig depend on the request. In a cached block, the framework checks them:

wp_is_user_logged_in() needs the variant LoggedInVary, RoleVary or UserVary.

wp_logout_url() contains a nonce of the user's session and cannot be used in cached blocks.

wp_date() without a timestamp and wp_human_time_diff() without a second timestamp depend on the current time and cannot be used in cached blocks.

A call that breaks these rules throws an error that names the block and the missing variant. Your own PHP code is not checked: if render() asks for the current user, declare UserVary yourself.

A REST route

A route that only reads data can be cached the same way. Put #[Cache] on the method:

#[RestRoute('/stats', HttpMethod::Get, new Capability('edit_posts'))]
#[Cache(ttl: 300, tags: [new TaxonomyTag('category')], vary: [new UserVary()])]
public function stats(int $limit = 10): array
{
    // …
}

The arguments of the request are part of the key: ?limit=5 and ?limit=20 get entries of their own. The permission check runs on every request, also when the response comes from the cache. Errors – a RestException or any other exception – are answered as usual and never stored.

A route may return a WP_REST_Response as well. The cache keeps its data, status and headers, but only for a status below 400: a deliberate 404 is answered every time, like an error.

A route may also take the WP_REST_Request. Only the arguments of the method are part of the key, though: whatever the route reads from the request beyond them – a header, a parameter it does not declare – must be declared as a variant, such as new HeaderVary('Accept-Language').

A cached route answers only GET.

Data of your own

For anything else, inject CacheStore and call remember(). It returns the cached value or calls your function, stores its result and returns it:

use Saij\WpAppFramework\Cache\CacheStore;

final readonly class Weather
{
    public function __construct(private CacheStore $cache, private WeatherClient $client) {}

    /**
     * @return array<string, mixed>
     */
    public function current(string $city): array
    {
        return $this->cache->remember(
            'weather-' . $city,
            fn(): array => $this->client->fetch($city),
            ttl: 600,
            tags: [Feed::Weather],
        );
    }
}

The key identifies the entry within your theme or plugin; include everything the value depends on, or declare it as a variant. Values must be plain data: null, booleans, numbers, strings and arrays of them. If your function throws, nothing is stored and the exception reaches you.

Queries of posts have a shortcut: Event::query()->…->cache(ttl: 600) caches their result with the tags of the post type and of the taxonomies they use (see Queries).

Rows of tables have no tag of the framework. To cache a value computed from a table, give it a tag of your own and invalidate that tag where your code saves or deletes rows, right after save().

Invalidating entries

Three tags are invalidated by the framework itself:

PostTypeTag('product') when a post of that type is created, changed, trashed, deleted, changes its status or its post meta. The edit lock the block editor sets while somebody edits a post does not count. Name your own post types by their post class: new PostTypeTag(Event::class).

TaxonomyTag('category') or TaxonomyTag(Category::class) when a term of that taxonomy is created, changed or deleted, changes its term meta, or is assigned to or removed from a post.

SettingsTag(SiteSettings::class) when the settings group is saved.

For everything else, define tags of your own. A tag is a case of a string-backed enum that implements CacheTag:

use Saij\WpAppFramework\Cache\CacheTag;

enum Feed: string implements CacheTag
{
    case Weather = 'weather';
}

Invalidate it with CacheStore::invalidate(), for example in a hook that runs when the external data changes:

$this->cache->invalidate(Feed::Weather);

Invalidating a tag does not delete anything. It gives the tag a new version, so the entries with the old version are no longer found and expire after their ttl. The versions are stored as options of your theme or plugin.

Where entries are stored

The framework stores entries in the first available backend of a list:

object: the persistent object cache, if the site has one (an object-cache.php drop-in such as Redis).

file: PHP files below wp-content/cache/{slug}/data, written atomically and read through OPcache. A daily WP-Cron event deletes expired files.

transient: transients in the database.

The site can change the list with the filter wp_app_framework/cache/backends/{slug}, for example in a must-use plugin. The values are plain strings, so the filter works without the theme's classes. An empty list turns the cache off:

add_filter('wp_app_framework/cache/backends/my-theme', fn(): array => ['transient']);
add_filter('wp_app_framework/cache/backends/my-plugin', fn(): array => []);

CacheStore::getBackendName() tells you which backend is used in the current request.

Variants

Variant	Value in the key
new UserVary()	ID of the current user, 0 for visitors who are not logged in
new LoggedInVary()	Whether the visitor is logged in
new RoleVary()	The roles of the current user
new UrlVary()	Path of the requested URL, without the query string
new QueryParamVary('page')	A parameter of the query string; a missing parameter differs from an empty one
new HeaderVary('Accept-Language')	A request header; a missing header differs from an empty one
new CookieVary('region')	A cookie; a missing cookie differs from an empty one
new ServiceVary(Region::class)	The value of a service of yours implementing VaryProvider (value(): string|int|float|bool|null)

Data sent with a POST request is no variant. A block that shows the result of a form submission must not be cached.

Rules

#[Cache(ttl, tags, vary)]:

Parameter	Type	Rule
ttl	int	Required; lifetime in seconds, at least 1.
tags	list<CacheTag>	PostTypeTag (a name of 1–20 characters or a post class), TaxonomyTag (a name of 1–32 characters or a taxonomy class), SettingsTag with a class that has #[SettingsGroup] in the same theme or plugin, or a case of a string-backed enum implementing CacheTag. No tag twice.
vary	list<CacheVary>	The variants above. QueryParamVary, HeaderVary and CookieVary need a name; the class of a ServiceVary must be a service implementing VaryProvider. No variant twice.

Build errors:

#[Cache] on a class without #[Block] or on a method without #[RestRoute].

A ttl below 1, an invalid tag or variant, a tag or variant listed twice.

A cached route that answers another method than GET, or declares a return type other than array, string, int, float, bool, null, WP_REST_Response or a union of them (void, other objects and mixed are errors).

At run time:

CacheStore::remember(string $key, Closure $compute, int $ttl, array $tags = [], array $vary = []) checks its arguments like the build; an empty key, an invalid ttl, tag or variant throws an InvalidArgumentException. A value that is not plain data throws a LogicException. A cached REST route whose data or headers are not plain data answers with status 500, like any other exception.

CacheStore::invalidate(CacheTag ...$tags) invalidates the tags of this theme or plugin.

The filter wp_app_framework/cache/backends/{slug} returns a list of 'object', 'file' and 'transient'; another value throws a LogicException.

Blocks are never cached in renders for the block editor, its preview or excerpts. Errors and REST responses with a status of 400 or more are never cached.
